Uncertain. Possibly from Late Latin coccum (“kernel, seed”), from Ancient Greek κόκκος (kókkos). Doublet of coque.
Learned borrowing from New Latin coccus, from Late Latin coccum, from Ancient Greek κόκκος (kókkos).
From Latin coriandrum, from Ancient Greek κορίανδρον (koríandron), alternative form of κορίαννον (koríannon).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin colla, from Ancient Greek κόλλα (kólla, “glue”). Compare Spanish cola, French colle, Italian colla.
Learned borrowing from Latin colossus, from Ancient Greek κολοσσός (kolossós).

parole.significato: collyrium, eyedrop (medicated liquid that is applied directly to the eyeball)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin collȳrium, from Ancient Greek κολλύριον (kollúrion).
Borrowed from Latin coma.
Learned borrowing from Latin comma, from Ancient Greek κόμμα (kómma).

parole.significato: comet (celestial body with a “tail” of matter)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin comēta, from Ancient Greek κομήτης (komḗtēs, “long-haired”).
From Vulgar Latin *concla, from Latin conchula, diminutive of concha, from Ancient Greek κόγχη (kónkhē), from Proto-Indo-European *kongʰo-

parole.significato: the butt of a spear or polearm
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin contus (“pike”), from Ancient Greek κοντός (kontós, “type of cavalry lance”).

parole.significato: coral (any of various species of anthozoans)
parole.testo: From Late Latin corallum or Latin corallium, from Ancient Greek κοράλλιον (korállion, “coral”), of uncertain origin.
From Latin chorda (“cord”), from Ancient Greek χορδή (khordḗ, “string of gut, the string of a lyre”).
Learned borrowing from Latin chorēa, borrowed from Ancient Greek χορεία (khoreía, “dance; circling motion”).

parole.significato: Korybant (any of a group of crested male dancers who worshipped the Phrygian goddess Cybele with drumming and dancing)
parole.testo: From Latin Corybantem, accusative of Corybās, from Ancient Greek Κορύβᾱς (Korúbās).

parole.significato: coryphaeus (leader of the chorus of a drama)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin coryphaeus, from Ancient Greek κορυφαῖος (koruphaîos, “leader of the chorus in an Ancient Greek drama”).
Borrowed from New Latin cormus, from Ancient Greek κορμός (kormós, “trunk stripped of its boughs”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese coro, probably borrowed from Latin chorus, from Ancient Greek χορός (khorós). Doublet of chorus.
From Old Galician-Portuguese corõa (“crown”), from Latin corōna, from Ancient Greek κορώνη (korṓnē, “garland, wreath”), from Proto-Indo-European *kor, *ker. Doublet of corona.
Borrowed from Latin corōna (“crown”). Doublet of coroa.
From Latin cothurnus and for extension Ancient Greek κόθορνος (kóthornos)

parole.significato: pot (trap used for fishing crabs and lobsters)
parole.testo: Alternation of côvão, an inheritance from Latin cophinus (“basket”), from Ancient Greek κόφινος (kóphinos, “basket”). Doublet of cobo.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin crānium, borrowed from Ancient Greek κρᾱνῐ́ον (krānĭ́on), from *κρᾱν- (*krān-) + -ῐ́ον (-ĭ́on).
Borrowed from Latin crypta, from Ancient Greek κρυπτός (kruptós). Doublet of gruta.
Borrowed from Latin crisis, from Ancient Greek κρίσις (krísis), from κρίνω (krínō, “pick out, choose, decide, judge”).

parole.significato: confirmation (sacrament of sealing one’s adhesion to the doctrine)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin chrisma, from Ancient Greek χρῖσμα (khrîsma).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cristal, crestal, from Latin crystallum (“crystal, ice”), from Ancient Greek κρύσταλλος (krústallos, “clear ice”), from κρύος (krúos, “frost”), from Proto-Indo-European *krus-, *kru- (“hard, hard outer surface, crust”).
From Latin Christianismus, from Ancient Greek χρῑστιᾱνισμός (khrīstiānismós).

Learned borrowing from Latin chrysostomus, from Ancient Greek χρυσόστομος (khrusóstomos, literally “golden-mouthed”), the epithet of John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople celebrated for his eloquence.

From New Latin criterion, from Ancient Greek κριτήριον (kritḗrion, “a test, a means of judging”), from κριτής (kritḗs, “a judge”), from κρίνω (krínō, “to judge”), from Proto-Indo-European *krey- (“to move, to separate”).
Borrowed from Latin crocus, from Ancient Greek κρόκος (krókos).
Learned borrowing from Latin crocodīlus, from Ancient Greek κροκόδειλος (krokódeilos).
From Latin chrōmaticus, from Ancient Greek χρωματικός (khrōmatikós), from χρῶμα (khrôma).
Borrowed from Latin crāpula.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin crānium, borrowed from Ancient Greek κρᾱνῐ́ον (krānĭ́on), from *κρᾱν- (*krān-) + -ῐ́ον (-ĭ́on).

parole.significato: crepida (a sandal with a simple sole and straps, used by the ancient Greeks and Romans)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin crepida, from Ancient Greek κρηπῑ́ς (krēpī́s).
Learned borrowing from Latin criticus, from Ancient Greek κριτικός (kritikós).
Learned borrowing from Latin chronicus, from Ancient Greek χρονικός (khronikós).
From Old Galician-Portuguese cuco, from Late Latin cucus or cuccus, or Latin cuculus or Ancient Greek κόκκυξ (kókkux).

parole.significato: object made from a reed, such as a pen or arrow
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin calamus (“reed, cane”).
Learned borrowing from New Latin calcium, a word derived by Sir Humphry Davy in 1808, from Latin calx (“lime, limestone”), supposedly from Ancient Greek χάλιξ (khálix, “pebble”).

parole.significato: calculus (differential calculus and integral calculus considered as a single subject)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin calculus (“pebble”), diminutive of calx (“limestone”), from Ancient Greek χάλιξ (khálix, “pebble”).
Learned borrowing from Latin calyx, from Ancient Greek κάλυξ (kálux).

parole.significato: chair; professorship (the office of a full professor, one who is not an associate professor)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cathedra. Doublet of cadeira.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese camara, from Vulgar Latin camara, from Latin camera, from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára).
Borrowed from Latin cannabis, from Ancient Greek κάνναβις (kánnabis). Doublet of cânhamo, cânave, and canvas.
Borrowed from Latin canōn, from Ancient Greek κανών (kanṓn, “measuring rod, standard”).

parole.significato: cantharus, a kind of Greco-Roman jug
parole.testo: From Latin cantharus (“cantharus”), from Ancient Greek κάνθαρος (kántharos, “cantharus”).

parole.significato: Celtic (of the Celts; of the style of the Celts)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin celticus (“Celtic”), from Celta (“Celt”), from Ancient Greek Κελτοί (Keltoí, “the Celts”).
From Latin cyclicus, from Ancient Greek κυκλικός (kuklikós). By surface analysis, ciclo + -ico.
Learned borrowing from Latin cymbalum.

parole.significato: cynical, cynic (of or relating to cynicism)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cynicus, from Ancient Greek κυνικός (kunikós).
Borrowed from Latin cithara, from Ancient Greek κιθάρα (kithára, “kind of harp”). Doublet of guitarra, which entered through Arabic, and of cítola and cistre.
Learned borrowing from Latin coccyx, from Ancient Greek κόκκυξ (kókkux, “cuckoo”).

parole.significato: cochlea (the complex, spirally coiled, tapered cavity of the inner ear)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cochlea, from Ancient Greek κοχλίας (kokhlías, “spiral, snail shell”).
Learned borrowing from Latin cholera, from Ancient Greek χολέρα (kholéra), from χολή (kholḗ, “bile”).
Learned borrowing from Latin cōlicus, from Ancient Greek κωλικός (kōlikós), from κῶλον (kôlon, “colon”).

parole.significato: colon (last part of the digestive system)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin colon (“large intestine”), from Ancient Greek κόλον (kólon, “the large intestine, also food, meat, fodder”).
From Latin cophinus (“basket”), from Ancient Greek κόφινος (kóphinos, “basket”). Compare Italian cofano, Spanish cuévano. Doublet of cofre. See also Portuguese covo, cobo.
From Old Galician-Portuguese demo (“demon; devil”), from Latin daemon (“demon”), from Ancient Greek δαίμων (daímōn, “god, goddess, divine power”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese demonio, from Latin daemonium, from Ancient Greek δαιμόνιον (daimónion), diminutive of δαίμων (daímōn, “god, divine power”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese diaboo, displacing the collateral forms diabre, diabro and diablo, from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin diabolus (“devil”) (probably borrowed as a semi-learned term), itself from Ancient Greek διάβολος (diábolos, “slanderer”). Doublet of diabolô and diábolo.
Learned borrowing from Latin diadēma, from Ancient Greek διάδημα (diádēma), from διαδέω (diadéō, “to bind around”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin diaphorēticus, from Ancient Greek διαφορητικός (diaphorētikós).
Learned borrowing from Latin dialectos.

Borrowed from Late Latin diamantem, from Latin adamantem, from Ancient Greek ἀδάμᾱς (adámās, “invincible, untamed; hard substance”), from ἀ- (a-, “un-”) + δαμάζω (damázō, “to overpower, tame, conquer”), from Proto-Indo-European *demh₂-.
Borrowed from Late Latin diarrhoea, from Ancient Greek διάρροια (diárrhoia, “through-flowing”), from διά (diá, “through”) + ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”).

parole.significato: diet (food a person or animal consumes)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin dieta (“regimen, regulation; assembly”), from Latin diaeta, from Ancient Greek δίαιτα (díaita). Doublet of diet.
Borrowed from Latin diaetēticus, from Ancient Greek διαιτητικός (diaitētikós).

parole.significato: dinosaur (any of various extinct reptiles belonging to the Dinosauria)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin dīnosaurus, from Ancient Greek δεινός (deinós, “terrible, awesome”) + σαῦρος (saûros, “lizard”).
Borrowed from Latin diplōma.

parole.significato: dys- (forms the names of conditions characterised by difficult or inadequate function)
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin dys-, from Ancient Greek δυσ- (dus-, “bad, hard”).

parole.significato: dysentery (disease characterised by inflammation of the intestines)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese desinteria, a learned borrowing from Latin dysenteria, borrowed from Ancient Greek δυσεντερία (dusentería), from δυσ- (dus-, “bad”) + ἔντερα (éntera, “bowels”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā).
Borrowed from New Latin dysprosium, from Ancient Greek δυσπρόσιτος (dusprósitos, “hard to get”).
Borrowed from Late Latin diūrēticus, from Ancient Greek διουρητικός (diourētikós), from διουρέω (diouréō, “to pass urine, have diuretic properties”).

parole.significato: deacon (a designated minister of charity in the early Church)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin diāconus, from Ancient Greek διᾱ́κονος (diā́konos).

parole.significato: dialogue (conversation or other discourse between individuals)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dialogus, from Ancient Greek διάλογος (diálogos).
Learned borrowing from Latin diametros, from Ancient Greek διάμετρος (diámetros, “measure across”).

parole.significato: diaeresis (separation of a vowel into two distinct syllables)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin diaeresis.

parole.significato: dogma (an indisputable and authoritative principle or belief)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dogma, from Ancient Greek δόγμα (dógma, “belief”).

parole.significato: dogmatic (stubbornly adhering to insufficiently proven beliefs)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin dogmaticus, from Ancient Greek δογματικός (dogmatikós).
Latin dosis, from Ancient Greek δόσις (dósis).

parole.significato: doxology (expression of praise to God, especially a short hymn)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin doxologia, from Ancient Greek δοξολογία (doxología, “a praising”), from δοξολόγος (doxológos, “giving or uttering praise”).
Borrowed from Latin drachma, from Ancient Greek δραχμή (drakhmḗ).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese dragon, from Latin dracōnem, from Ancient Greek δράκων (drákōn). Cognate with Galician and Spanish dragón and also English drake.
From Late Latin drāma, from Ancient Greek δρᾶμα (drâma, “an act, a theatrical act, a play”). Doublet of dorama.
From Late Latin drāmaticus, from Ancient Greek δραματικός (dramatikós).
From Latin Dryadem, from Ancient Greek Δρυάς (Druás, “dryad, tree nymph”).

parole.significato: ten (set or group with ten elements)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin decādem, from Ancient Greek δεκάς (dekás).
Learned borrowing from Latin Daedalus, from Ancient Greek Δαίδαλος (Daídalos), named after the inventor of the maze in Greek mythology.
From Late Latin diptycha, plural, from Ancient Greek, neuter plural of δίπτυχος (díptukhos, “folded, doubled”), from δι (di) + -πτυχος (-ptukhos) (akin to Greek πτυχή (ptychí, “fold, layer”)).
Borrowed from Late Latin ecclēsiasticus (“of the church”), from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησιαστικός (ekklēsiastikós), from ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía).
Borrowed from Latin eclīpsis, from Ancient Greek ἔκλειψις (ékleipsis, “eclipse”).
Borrowed from New Latin eclampsia, from Ancient Greek ἔκλᾰμψῐς (éklămpsĭs, “sudden development, violent onset”, literally “brightness”).

parole.significato: ecclesia (the public legislative assembly of Athens)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ecclēsia, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía), from ἔκκλητος (ékklētos) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā). Doublet of igreja, which was inherited.

parole.significato: echo (a reflected sound that is heard again by its initial observer)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin echō, from Ancient Greek ἠχώ (ēkhṓ), from ἠχή (ēkhḗ, “sound”), from Proto-Indo-European *sweh₂gʰ-.
Borrowed from Latin oeconomia, from Ancient Greek οἰκονομία (oikonomía, “management of a household, administration”), from οἶκος (oîkos, “house”) + νόμος (nómos, “law”).

parole.significato: ecumenical (pertaining to the Christian Church worldwide)
parole.testo: From Late Latin oecūmenicus, from Ancient Greek οἰκουμενικός (oikoumenikós).

parole.significato: eczema (acute or chronic inflammation of the skin)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin eczema, from Ancient Greek ἔκζεμα (ékzema).

parole.significato: oedema (excessive accumulation of serum in tissue)
parole.testo: From New Latin edema, from Ancient Greek οἴδημα (oídēma, “swelling”), from οἰδέω (oidéō, “to swell”).

parole.significato: Aegean (of or relating to the Aegean Sea)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aegaeus, from Ancient Greek Αἰγαῖος (Aigaîos, “Aegean”).

parole.significato: Egyptian (of, from or relating to Egypt)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese egípcio, a learned borrowing from Latin aegyptius, borrowed from Ancient Greek Αἰγύπτιος (Aigúptios).

parole.significato: elephant (any mammal of the order Proboscidea)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese elefante, elifante, borrowed from Latin elephantis (“elephant”), from Ancient Greek ἐλέφᾱς (eléphās, “elephant, ivory”). Doublet of olifante.
Learned borrowing from Latin elephantiasis, from Ancient Greek ἐλεφᾰντῐ́ᾱσῐς (elephăntĭ́āsĭs).
From Latin elegīa, from Ancient Greek ἐλεγεία (elegeía).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin elenchus, from Ancient Greek ἔλεγχος (élenkhos). Compare Italian and Spanish elenco.
Learned borrowing from Latin ēlogium (“inscription on a tombstone”), from Ancient Greek ἐλεγεῖον (elegeîon, “elegiac poem or inscription”).
Learned borrowing from Latin aelūrus (“cat”) from Ancient Greek αἴλουρος (aílouros, “cat”).

From New Latin elasticus (“elastic”), from Ancient Greek as if *ἐλαστής (*elastḗs) for ἐλατής (elatḗs), equivalent to ἐλατήρ (elatḗr, “a driver, hurler”), from ἐλαύνειν (elaúnein, “to drive, set in motion, push, strike, beat out”).

parole.significato: elliptical (in shape reminding of an ellipse, oval)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ellīpticus, from Ancient Greek ἐλλειπτικός (elleiptikós, “defective”).
From Latin emblēma, from Ancient Greek ἔμβλημα (émblēma, “insertion”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin embryon, from Ancient Greek ἔμβρυον (émbruon, “fetus”), from ἐν (en, “in-”) + βρύω (brúō, “to grow, to swell”).

parole.significato: empirical (pertaining to or based on experience)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin empiricus.
Borrowed from Latin emporium (“market”), from Ancient Greek ἐμπορεῖον (emporeîon), from ἔμπορος (émporos, “marketer”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + πόρος (póros, “travel”).

parole.significato: encyclopedia (reference work consisting of a list of words or expressions, not always arranged in alphabetical order, i…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin encyclopaedia (“general education”), a univerbated form of Koine Greek ἐγκύκλιος παιδείᾱ (enkúklios paideíā), from ἐγκύκλιος (enkúklios) + παιδείᾱ (paideíā).
From Late Latin encliticus, from Ancient Greek ἐγκλιτικός (enklitikós).

parole.significato: to encrypt (conceal information by means of a code or cipher)
parole.testo: From English encrypt + -ar, from en- + crypt, from Latin crypta (“vault”), from Ancient Greek κρυπτός (kruptós, “hidden”), from κρύπτω (krúptō, “to conceal”), from Proto-Indo-European *krāu-.
Internationalism. Learned borrowing from New Latin encephalon, from Ancient Greek ἐγκέφαλος (enképhalos, “within the head”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese ãedlo, from Vulgar Latin *anēthulum, diminutive of anēthum, from Ancient Greek ἄνηθον (ánēthon). Cognate with Spanish eneldo.

parole.significato: enema (injection of fluid into the rectum)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin enema, from Ancient Greek ἔνεμα (énema, “injection”), from ἐνίημι (eníēmi, “to send in, inject”).

Learned borrowing from Latin energīa (“energy”), from Ancient Greek ἐνέργεια (enérgeia, “action, act, work”), from ἐνεργός (energós, “active”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”), from Proto-Indo-European *wérǵom.

parole.significato: emphyteusis (long-term right to use a property on condition of taking care of it and paying taxes)
parole.testo: From Latin emphyteusis, from Ancient Greek ἐμφύτευσις (emphúteusis, “tenure of a type of leasehold”).
Borrowed from Latin aenigma (“riddle”), from Ancient Greek αἴνιγμα (aínigma, “dark saying, riddle”).
Borrowed from Late Latin entelechīa, from Ancient Greek ἐντελέχεια (entelékheia).
Learned borrowing from Latin entheus, from Ancient Greek ἔνθεος (éntheos).

parole.significato: enthymeme (syllogism in which a premise or conclusion is implied)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin enthȳmēma, from Ancient Greek ἐνθύμημα (enthúmēma).

Borrowed from Late Latin enthūsiasmus, from Ancient Greek ἐνθουσιασμός (enthousiasmós, “inspiration, enthusiasm”), from ἔνθεος (éntheos, “possessed by a god”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + θεός (theós, “god”).
Borrowed from Latin ē̆ōus, from Ancient Greek ἠῷος (ēōîos), ἑῷος (heōîos, “of the east; of the morning”), derived from ἠώς (ēṓs, “dawn”). Compare English eoan, Italian eoo.
From Latin epicoenus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίκοινος (epíkoinos), based on κοινός (koinós, “common”).

parole.significato: epicycle (a small circle whose centre is on the circumference of a larger circle)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin epicy̆clus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίκυκλος (epíkuklos). By surface analysis, epi- + ciclo.
Borrowed from Latin epidēmia, from Ancient Greek ἐπιδήμιος (epidḗmios), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + δῆμος (dêmos, “people”).
Borrowed from Latin epidermis (“epidermis”), from Ancient Greek ἐπιδερμίς (epidermís), from ἐπί (epí, “on top of”) + δέρμα (dérma, “skin”).

parole.significato: epiglottis (cartilaginous organ in the throat of terrestrial vertebrates)
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin epiglōttis. By surface analysis, epi- + glote.
Learned borrowing from Latin epilēpsia, from Ancient Greek ἐπιληψία (epilēpsía), from ἐπιλαμβάνω (epilambánō, “to seize”).
Learned borrowing from Latin epilēpticus. By surface analysis, epilepsia + -ico.

Latin epithalamium, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐπιθαλάμιον (epithalámion, “bridal song”), neuter form of ἐπιθαλάμιος (epithalámios), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + θάλαμος (thálamos, “inner chamber, wedding chamber”).
From modern Latin epizeuxis, from Ancient Greek ἐπίζευξις (epízeuxis, “a fastening upon”), from ἐπιζευγνύναι (epizeugnúnai), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + ζευγνύναι (zeugnúnai, “to yoke”).

parole.significato: a bishop, especially during the early Christian church
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin episcopus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos). Doublet of bispo.
Borrowed from Late Latin epistola, from Ancient Greek ἐπιστολή (epistolḗ).

Borrowed from Latin epitheton, from Ancient Greek ἐπίθετον (epítheton), neuter form of ἐπίθετος (epíthetos, “added”), from ἐπιτίθημι (epitíthēmi, “to add on”), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “to put, to place”).
Learned borrowing from Latin echīnus, from Ancient Greek ἐχῖνος (ekhînos).
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin erēmīta, from Ancient Greek ἐρημίτης (erēmítēs).
From Scientific Latin erythema, from Ancient Greek ἐρύθημα (erúthēma).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ermo, hermo, from Late Latin eremus, from Latin erēmus, from Ancient Greek ἔρημος (érēmos), with preservation of Greek accent over vowel length in Late Latin. Compare Aromanian ermu
Learned borrowing from Latin erōticus, from Ancient Greek ἐρωτῐκός (erōtĭkós).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin scandalizō, from Ancient Greek σκανδαλίζω (skandalízō). By surface analysis, escândalo + -izar.
From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Latin scarabaeus (“beetle”), from Ancient Greek κάραβος (kárabos, “beetle”).
Borrowed from New Latin sclera, from Ancient Greek σκληρός (sklērós, “hard”).

parole.significato: school (institution dedicated to teaching and learning)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese escola, from Latin schola, from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ, “spare time, leisure”). The Portuguese form may indicate a semi-learned influence on the phonetic aspects of the word.

parole.significato: scholastic (relating to scholasticism, medieval philosophical system)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin scholasticus, from Ancient Greek σχολᾰστῐκός (skholăstĭkós).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese escorpiõ, from Latin scorpiōnem (“scorpion”), from Ancient Greek σκορπίος (skorpíos).
Learned borrowing from Latin scandalum, from Ancient Greek σκάνδαλον (skándalon), from Proto-Indo-European *skand- (“to jump”).
Borrowed from Latin scoria, from Ancient Greek σκωρία (skōría).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin sphēra, from Latin sphaera, borrowed from Ancient Greek σφαῖρᾰ (sphaîră, “ball, globe”).
Learned borrowing from Latin sphingem, from Ancient Greek Σφίγξ (Sphínx).
Learned borrowing from Latin sphaericus. By surface analysis, esfera + -ico.
Learned borrowing from Latin smēgma.

parole.significato: alms (small amount of money or goods given to someone as charity)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese esmolla, esmolna, earlier elmosna, from Late Latin eleēmosyna, from Ancient Greek ἐλεημοσύνη (eleēmosúnē).
From Medieval Latin sparagus, asparagus, from Ancient Greek ἀσπάραγος (aspáragos).
Borrowed from Latin spasmus, from Ancient Greek σπασμός (spasmós).
From Latin spēlunca, from Ancient Greek σπῆλυγξ (spêlunx), from earlier σπέος (spéos).
Learned borrowing from New Latin splanchnicus, from Ancient Greek σπλαγχνικός (splankhnikós), from σπλάγχνα (splánkhna, “viscera”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”).

From Late Latin spora, from Ancient Greek σπόρος (spóros, “sowing”) and σπείρω (speírō, “to sow”), from Proto-Indo-European *sper- (“to strew”).
Inherited from Latin sporadicus, borrowed from Ancient Greek σποραδικός (sporadikós).

Borrowed from Latin schēma, from Ancient Greek σχῆμα (skhêma, “form, shape”).

parole.significato: stasis (slowing or stoppage of the normal flow of a bodily fluid)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin stasis, from Ancient Greek στάσις (stásis).

parole.significato: stele (upright slab containing engraved or painted decorations or inscriptions)
parole.testo: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin stēla (“pillar”), from Ancient Greek στήλη (stḗlē).

Borrowed from Latin stratēgēma, from Ancient Greek στρατήγημα (stratḗgēma).

parole.significato: strategy (science and art of military command)
parole.testo: Derived from Latin strategia, from Ancient Greek στρᾰτηγῐ́ᾱ (strătēgĭ́ā).

parole.significato: heat (condition where a mammal is aroused sexually or where it is especially fertile)
parole.testo: From Latin oestrus, from Ancient Greek οἶστρος (oîstros, “vehement desire, frenzy”, literally “gadfly”).
Learned borrowing from Latin stadium (“stadium for footraces, stade”), from Ancient Greek στάδιον (stádion).
Inherited from Latin stomachus, from Ancient Greek στόμαχος (stómakhos), from στόμα (stóma, “mouth”).

parole.significato: Ethiopian (of, from, or pertaining to Ethiopia)

Learned borrowing from Latin eunuchus, from Ancient Greek εὐνοῦχος (eunoûkhos).

parole.significato: euro (currency unit of the European Union)
parole.testo: Clipping of Europa, from Latin Eurōpa, from Ancient Greek Εὐρώπη (Eurṓpē).

parole.significato: European (related to Europe or the European Union)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Eurōpaeus, borrowed from Ancient Greek Εὐρωπαῖος (Eurōpaîos), from Εὐρώπᾱ (Eurṓpā, “Europe”) + -ῐος (-ĭos, “belonging to”). By surface analysis, Europa + -eu.
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin ēvangelium, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion, “good news”).

parole.significato: to evangelize (preach the Christian gospel, especially to non-Christians)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin ēvangelizāre, from Ancient Greek.
Learned borrowing from Latin exēgēticum, from Ancient Greek ἐξηγητικός (exēgētikós)

parole.significato: exoteric (said of a philosophical doctrine intended to be expounded in public)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin exōtericus, from Ancient Greek ἐξωτερῐκός (exōterĭkós).

parole.significato: a cabinet where medicine is stored
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin pharmacia, from Ancient Greek φαρμακεία (pharmakeía, “the use of drugs”), from φάρμακον (phármakon, “a drug, charm, enchantment”).

Learned borrowing from Latin Phoenīcius (“phoenician”), from Phoenīcia (“Phoenicia”), from Ancient Greek Φοινίκη (Phoiníkē), from φοίνικι (phoíniki, “Phoenicians”), from Mycenaean Greek 𐀡𐀛𐀑𐀍 (po-ni-ki-jo), from Egyptian fnḫw (fenekhu, “Canaanites, Syrians”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin phaenomenon, from Ancient Greek φαινόμενον (phainómenon, “thing appearing to view”).

parole.significato: philanthropy (benevolent altruism with the intention of increasing the well-being of mankind)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin philanthrōpia, from Ancient Greek φιλανθρωπία (philanthrōpía).

parole.significato: phylum (rank below kingdom and above class)

Borrowed from Latin phlegma, from Ancient Greek φλέγμα (phlégma, “flame”). Doublet of freima.

parole.significato: earless seal (any seal in the family Phocidae)

parole.significato: genealogy (the descent of a person, family, or group from an ancestor or ancestors)

parole.significato: geography (study of physical structure and inhabitants of the Earth)

parole.significato: genesis (the origin, start, or point at which something comes into being)

From Latin hieraticus, from Ancient Greek ἱερατικός (hieratikós).

parole.significato: isometry (function in which the distance between two images is equal to the distance between their pre-images)
parole.testo: From Latin isometria, from Ancient Greek.
From New Latin ischaemia, from Ancient Greek ἴσχαιμος (ískhaimos, “stoppage of blood flow”), from ῐ̓́σχω (ĭ́skhō, “to hold back, restrain; to stay, stop”) + αἷμᾰ (haîmă, “blood”).

parole.significato: someone from the State of Israel
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Isrāēlīta, from Ancient Greek Ἰσρᾱηλῑ́της (Isrāēlī́tēs). By surface analysis, Israel + -ita.

parole.significato: isthmus (narrow strip of land connecting two larger landmasses)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin isthmus, from Ancient Greek ῐ̓σθμός (ĭsthmós, “neck”).
From Latin hyacinthus, from Ancient Greek ὑάκινθος (huákinthos, “any of several dark blue flowers”).
Borrowed from Latin iaspis, from Ancient Greek ἴασπις (íaspis).

parole.significato: Used to express surprise, excitement or exasperation.
parole.testo: Relatinised from Old Galician-Portuguese Jesu, from Latin Iēsūs, from Ancient Greek Ἰησοῦς (Iēsoûs), from Hebrew ישוע (yeshúa).

parole.significato: The name of the Latin script letter J/j.
parole.testo: From Latin iota, from Ancient Greek ἰῶτα (iôta, “iota”), from Semitic. Doublet of iota.
Borrowed from Late Latin iūdaismus, from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαϊσμός (Ioudaïsmós), from Hebrew יְהוּדָה (Yehuda, “Judah”).

parole.significato: Jew, Jewish person (adherent of Judaism or member or descendant of the Jewish people)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese judeu (“Jew”), from Latin iūdaeus (“Jew; Judaean”), from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαῖος (Ioudaîos), from Hebrew יהודי (Yehudi). By surface analysis, Judeia + -eu. Displaced the collateral form judio.

parole.significato: labyrinth, maze (complicated irregular network of passages or paths)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin labyrinthus, from Ancient Greek λαβύρινθος (labúrinthos).

parole.significato: laconic (using as few words as possible)
parole.testo: From Latin Lacōnicus (“Spartan”), from Ancient Greek Λακωνικός (Lakōnikós, “Laconian”).

parole.significato: litany (prayers recited by a leader alternated with responses from the congregation)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ledaỹa, from Latin litanīa, from Ancient Greek λιτανεία (litaneía, “prayer”). Cognate with Galician ladaíña. Doublet of litania.

parole.significato: layman (someone who is not an ordained cleric)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin lāicus. Doublet of the inherited leigo.

parole.significato: lambdacism (substituting an L for an R)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lambdacismus, from Ancient Greek λᾰβδᾰκῐσμός (lăbdăkĭsmós).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese lanterna, from Latin lanterna (“lantern; lamp”), corruption of Ancient Greek λαμπτήρ (lamptḗr, “torch”).
From laringe (“larynx”) + -ite (“-itis”), from Latin larynx, from Ancient Greek λάρυγξ (lárunx).

parole.significato: layman (someone who is not an ordained cleric)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese leigo, from Latin lāicus (“lay; unconsecrated”), from Ancient Greek λαϊκός (laïkós, “of the people”), from λαός (laós, “the people”). Doublet of laico.
Learned borrowing from Latin lemma, from Ancient Greek λῆμμα (lêmma). Compare Spanish lema.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin leopardus from Ancient Greek λεόπαρδος (leópardos) from λέων (léōn, “lion”) + πάρδος (párdos, “panther”).

parole.significato: leprosy (infectious disease caused by infection by Mycobacterium leprae)
parole.testo: From Latin lepra (“leprosy”), from Ancient Greek λέπρα (lépra, “leprosy”), from λεπίς (lepís, “scale”), from λέπω (lépō, “to peel”).
Borrowed from Late Latin levisticum, probably an alteration of Latin ligusticum, from Ligusticus (“Ligurian”), ultimately from Ancient Greek Λίγυς (Lígus).
From Old Galician-Portuguese leon (“lion”), from Latin leōnem (“lion”), from Ancient Greek λέων (léōn). Doublet of leu. Cognate with Galician and Spanish león among others.
Borrowed from Latin Lyceum, from Ancient Greek Λύκειον (Lúkeion).
From Latin leinteria, from Ancient Greek λειεντερία (leientería).
Learned borrowing from Latin lyncem, from Ancient Greek λύγξ (lúnx), from Proto-Indo-European *leuk- (“to shine, bright, to see”). Displaced Old Galician-Portuguese lĩis. Doublet of onça.

parole.significato: lymph (fluid carried by the lymphatic system)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin lympha, from Ancient Greek νύμφη (númphē).
Learned borrowing from Latin lysis, from Ancient Greek λύσις (lúsis).

parole.significato: litotes (an understatement employed for rhetoric effect)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin lītotēs, from Ancient Greek λιτότης (litótēs).

parole.significato: liturgy (a predetermined or prescribed set of rituals)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin lītūrgia, from Ancient Greek λειτουργία (leitourgía).
Learned borrowing from New Latin lobus, from Ancient Greek λοβός (lobós, “earlobe”).

parole.significato: lochus, lochos (a corps of troops among the Greeks)
parole.testo: From Latin lochus, from Ancient Greek λόχος (lókhos, “a company of troops”).
Borrowed from Latin lōtus, from Ancient Greek λωτός (lōtós).

parole.significato: logistic (relating to the transportation of goods or supplies)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin logisticus, from Ancient Greek λογιστικός (logistikós).
Borrowed from Latin lōtus, from Ancient Greek λωτός (lōtós).

From Old Galician-Portuguese lampada, borrowed from Late Latin lampada, from Latin lampas, from Ancient Greek λαμπάς (lampás, “lamp or flambeau”), from Ancient Greek λάμπω (lámpō, “to shine”). Compare the inherited Old Portuguese form lampaa.
Borrowed from Latin līchēn, from Ancient Greek λειχήν (leikhḗn), from λείχω (leíkhō, “to lick”).
Learned borrowing from Latin lyricus, from Ancient Greek λυρικός (lurikós), from λύρα (lúra, “lyre”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese liro, lílio, from Latin līlium, from Ancient Greek λείριον (leírion). Doublet of lis.
Borrowed from Latin lōtus, from Ancient Greek λωτός (lōtós).

From Latin logica, from Ancient Greek λογική (logikḗ, “logic”), from the feminine form of λογικός (logikós, “of or relating to speech or reason or reasoning, rational, reasonable”), from λόγος (lógos, “speech, reason”).

parole.significato: logical (in agreement with the principles of logic)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin logicus.

parole.significato: lotus (an aquatic flowering plant of the genus Nelumbo)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lōtus, from Ancient Greek λωτός (lōtós).
Borrowed from Latin macedonicus.
From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Latin mataxa, from Ancient Greek μέταξα (métaxa).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin magia, from Ancient Greek μαγεία (mageía).
Borrowed from Latin magma, from Ancient Greek μάγμα (mágma, “paste”).
Borrowed from Latin magus, from Ancient Greek μάγος (mágos), from Old Iranian.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *madiga, from Latin magida, from Ancient Greek μαγίδα (magída).
Borrowed from Latin mania or Ancient Greek μανία (manía, “madness”).
Possibly a derivative of Late Latin basilicum, from Ancient Greek βασιλικόν (basilikón).
Borrowed from Late Latin maniacus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μανιακός (maniakós), adjectival form of μανία (manía, “madness”). See mania.

parole.significato: to engineer (to plan or achieve a goal by contrivance or guile)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin māchinārī (“scheme, plot”), a verb based on Latin māchina (“device, scheme”), an early borrowing from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: daisy (Bellis perennis, a wild flower with a yellow head and white petals)
parole.testo: From Latin margarīta (“pearl”), from Ancient Greek μαργαρίτης (margarítēs). Doublet of margarita, marguerita, and Margarete.
From Latin margarīta, from Ancient Greek μαργαρίτης (margarítēs).

From Old Galician-Portuguese marmelo, from Latin melimēlum (“sweet apple”), from Ancient Greek μελίμηλον (melímēlon), from μέλι (méli, “honey”) + μῆλον (mêlon, “apple”). Compare Fala marmelu, Galician marmelo and Spanish membrillo.
Learned borrowing from Latin marsūpium, from Ancient Greek μαρσίππιον (marsíppion), diminutive of μάρσιππος (mársippos, “pouch”).
Learned borrowing from Latin martyrium, from Ancient Greek μαρτύριον (martúrion, “testimony”). Displaced Old Galician-Portuguese marteiro.

parole.significato: dough (a thick, malleable substance made by mixing flour with other ingredients)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese massa, from Latin massa (“mass; dough”), from Ancient Greek μᾶζα (mâza, “bread”), from μάσσω (mássō, “to handle; to knead”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂ǵ-.
Learned borrowing from Latin mathēmaticus, from Ancient Greek μαθηματικός (mathēmatikós), from μάθημα (máthēma, “knowledge, learning”).

parole.significato: mechanism (mechanical means for the conversion or control of motion)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin mechanismus.
Learned borrowing from Latin mēchanicum.
From Old Galician-Portuguese meigo, from Latin magicus (“magical”), from Ancient Greek μαγικός (magikós). Doublet of mágico, a borrowing. Cf. also Leonese meigo; compare Galician meigo, Spanish mego.
From Old Galician-Portuguese melanconia, borrowed from Late Latin melancholia, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολία (melankholía, “blackness of the bile”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin melancholicus, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολικός (melankholikós).

parole.significato: melody (sequence of notes that makes up a musical phrase)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin melōdia (“melody”), from Ancient Greek μελῳδίᾱ (melōidíā, “singing, chanting”), from μέλος (mélos, “musical phrase”) + ἀοιδή (aoidḗ, “song”), contracted form ᾠδή (ōidḗ).

parole.significato: melopoeia (the sound of words as a facet of poetry)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin melopoeia, from Ancient Greek μελοποιΐα (melopoiḯa), from μελοποιός (melopoiós, “song-maker, lyric poet”).

parole.significato: mint (any plant of the family Lamiaceae)
parole.testo: From Latin menta, mentha, from Ancient Greek μίνθη (mínthē).

parole.significato: messiah (person ordained by God to lead the people of Israel)
parole.testo: From Latin Messīās.

parole.significato: metonymy (the use of a single characteristic or name of an object to identify the entire object)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin metonymia, from Ancient Greek μετωνυμίᾱ (metōnumíā, “change of name”), from μετά (metá, “other”) + ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”).
Learned borrowing from Latin mētropolis, from Ancient Greek μητρόπολις (mētrópolis).

parole.significato: metaphor (the use of a word or phrase to refer to something other than its literal meaning)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin metaphora, from Ancient Greek μεταφορά (metaphorá).
Borrowed from Latin miasma, from Ancient Greek μίασμα (míasma, “pollution”).
Learned borrowing from New Latin myosotis, from Ancient Greek μυοσωτίς (muosōtís, “mouse's ear; forget-me-not”).

parole.significato: myrrh (dried sap of the Commiphora myrrha tree)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese mirra, from Latin myrrha, from Ancient Greek μύρρα (múrrha), of Semitic origin.
Learned borrowing from Latin myrtus, from Ancient Greek μύρτος (múrtos).
Borrowed from Latin mystagōgus, from Ancient Greek μυσταγωγός (mustagōgós).

Learned borrowing from Latin mystērium, from Ancient Greek μυστήριον (mustḗrion, “a mystery, a secret, a secret rite”), from μύστης (mústēs, “initiated one”), from μυέω (muéō, “to initiate”), from μύω (múō, “to shut”).
Learned borrowing from Latin mitra, from Ancient Greek μίτρα (mítra).

parole.significato: A small boat, uncovered and powered by oars, used by guards to watch the coasts of pirate invasions.
parole.testo: From Latin myoparō, from Ancient Greek μυοπάρων (muopárōn).
Learned borrowing from Latin mnēmonicus, from Ancient Greek μνημονικός (mnēmonikós, “of memory”), from μνήμων (mnḗmōn, “remembering, mindful”), from μνάομαι (mnáomai, “to remember”).
Borrowed from Late Latin monarcha, from Ancient Greek μονάρχης (monárkhēs), variant of μόναρχος (mónarkhos, “sole ruler”).

parole.significato: monarchy (form of government with a hereditary head of state)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin monarchia, from Ancient Greek μοναρχία (monarkhía). By surface analysis, mono- + -arquia.
Learned borrowing from Latin monastērium, from Ancient Greek μοναστήριον (monastḗrion). Doublet of mosteiro.

parole.significato: monogamy (form of relationship in which an individual has only one partner during their lifetime or at any one time)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin monogamia, from Ancient Greek μονογαμία (monogamía). By surface analysis, mono- + -gamia.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin monosyllabicus, from Latin monosyllabus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek μονοσύλλαβος (monosúllabos). By surface analysis, mono- + silábico.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin monasticus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin monotonus, from Ancient Greek μονότονος (monótonos).

parole.significato: moray (any eel of the family Muraenidae)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese *morẽa, from Latin murēna, from Ancient Greek μῡ́ραινα (mū́raina). Cognate with Galician morea.

Learned borrowing from Latin mortiferum, derived from mors (“death”) + -fer (“-bearing, -carrying”), originally a calque of Ancient Greek θᾰνᾰτηφόρος (thănătēphóros, “deadly, lethal”, literally “death-bearing”). By surface analysis, morte + -ífero.

From Old Galician-Portuguese mõesteiro (“monastery”), from Vulgar Latin *monistērium from Late Latin monastērium (“monastery, monk's cell”), from Ancient Greek μοναστήριον (monastḗrion, “hermit's cell”), from μόνος (mónos, “alone”). Cognate with Galician mosteiro, English minster and French moutier

parole.significato: Moorish (of or relating to the Moors)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mouro (“Moor”), from Latin Maurus (“Moor”), from Ancient Greek μαυρός (maurós, “dark”). Doublet of Mauro and moro.

parole.significato: myrtle (evergreen shrub of the genus Myrtus)
parole.testo: From Latin myrta (“myrtle”), from Ancient Greek μύρτος (múrtos, “myrtle”), from a Semitic root M-R-R meaning "bitter".
Learned borrowing from Latin mūsa, from Ancient Greek Μοῦσα (Moûsa, “Muse”).
Learned borrowing from Latin mūsēum (“library, study”), from Ancient Greek Μουσεῖον (Mouseîon), shrine of the Muses (Μοῦσα (Moûsa)).
Borrowed from Latin magicus, from Ancient Greek μαγικός (magikós), from μάγος (mágos, “wise man, mage”). Compare meigo, which is likely a doublet.
From Old Galician-Portuguese marmor, from Vulgar Latin *marmŏrem, from Latin marmor n, from Ancient Greek μάρμαρος (mármaros, “marble”).
From Ecclesiastical Latin martyr, from Ancient Greek μάρτυς (mártus, “witness”).
Learned borrowing from Latin methodus, from Ancient Greek μέθοδος (méthodos).

parole.significato: metric (of or relating to the metric system)
parole.testo: From Latin metricus, from Ancient Greek μετρικός (metrikós).

parole.significato: mystic; mystical (relating to mystics, mysticism or occult mysteries)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin mysticus, from Ancient Greek μυστικός (mustikós, “secret, mystic”).

parole.significato: musician (a person who composes, plays or sings music)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin mūsicus (“musician; pertaining to music”), from Ancient Greek μουσικός (mousikós, “musical”).

parole.significato: narcissus; daffodil (any of several bulbous flowering plants of the genus Narcissus)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin narcissus, from Ancient Greek νάρκισσος (nárkissos).
Learned borrowing from Latin nauta, from Ancient Greek ναύτης (naútēs).
Learned borrowing from Latin neophytus, from Ancient Greek νεόφυτος (neóphutos).
Learned borrowing from Latin nympha, from Ancient Greek νύμφη (númphē, “young woman, nymph”).
From Latin nitrum, from Ancient Greek νίτρον (nítron).
Borrowed from Late Latin nosocomīum, from Ancient Greek νοσοκομεῖον (nosokomeîon, “hospital”), from νόσος (nósos, “disease, illness”) + κομέω (koméō, “to take care of”).
From New Latin nostalgia, coined from Ancient Greek νόστος (nóstos, “returning home”) + ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”). Cognate with Galician nostalxia.
From Latin Nāïas, from Ancient Greek Νᾱϊάς (Nāïás, “naiad”), from νάειν (náein, “to flow”).

parole.significato: nausea (feeling of physical unwellness, usually with the desire to vomit)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nausea, nausia, from Ancient Greek ναυσία (nausía, “seasickness”), from ναῦς (naûs, “ship”).
Borrowed from Latin nauticus, from Ancient Greek ναυτικός (nautikós), from ναύτης (naútēs) "sailor".

parole.significato: nautilus (any marine mollusc of the family Nautilidae)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin nautilus.
Learned borrowing from Latin nectar, from Ancient Greek νέκταρ (néktar), from Proto-Indo-European *néḱtr̥h₂, derived from the roots *neḱ- (“to perish, disappear”) and *terh₂- (“to overcome”).
From Latin mespilum, from Ancient Greek μέσπιλον (méspilon).

parole.significato: obelisk (a tall stone monolith topped with a pyramidal point)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin obeliscus, from Ancient Greek ὀβελίσκος (obelískos).
Learned borrowing from Latin Oceanus, from Ancient Greek Ὠκεανός (Ōkeanós, “Oceanus, a water deity”).
Borrowed from Latin octaedros, from Ancient Greek ὀκτάεδρος (oktáedros), from Ancient Greek ὀκτώ (oktṓ, “eight”) + ἕδρα (hédra, “seat”). By surface analysis, octa- + -edro.
Learned borrowing from Latin ōda.
Earlier ophídio, from Latin Ophidia, from Ancient Greek ὄφις (óphis, “snake”).
Borrowed from Late Latin oligarcha, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγάρχης (oligárkhēs).
Borrowed from Late Latin oligarchia, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγαρχία (oligarkhía). By surface analysis, oligarca + -ia or oligo- + -arquia
Learned borrowing from Late Latin oligarchicus, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγαρχικός (oligarkhikós). By surface analysis, oligarquia (“oligarchy”) + -ico (“-ic”, adjective-forming suffix).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin onagra, from Ancient Greek ὀνάγρα (onágra).
Learned borrowing from Latin onagrus, borrowed from Ancient Greek ὄναγρος (ónagros, “wild ass”), from ὄνος (ónos, “ass, donkey”) + ᾰ̓́γρῐος (ắgrĭos, “wild”).

parole.significato: onomatopoeia (property of a word of sounding like what it represents)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin onomatopoeïa, from Ancient Greek ὀνοματοποιία (onomatopoiía, “the coining of a word in imitation of a sound”).
Unadapted borrowing from Latin orchēstra, borrowed from Ancient Greek ὀρχήστρα (orkhḗstra), from ὀρχέομαι (orkhéomai, “to dance”) + -τρᾰ (-tră, “a suffix used to form instrument nouns (pl.)”).
From New Latin Orchideae, Orchidaceae, an irregular formation from Latin orchis, from Ancient Greek ὄρχις (órkhis, “orchid, testicle”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin orthodoxia, from Ancient Greek ὀρθοδοξία (orthodoxía, “right opinion”). By surface analysis, ortodoxo + -ia.

parole.significato: orthodox (adhering to established religious doctrine or tradition)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin orthodoxus, from Ancient Greek ὀρθόδοξος (orthódoxos, “having the right opinion”). By surface analysis, orto- + -doxo.
From Latin orthographia, from Ancient Greek ὀρθογραφία (orthographía), from ὀρθός (orthós, “correct”) and γράφω (gráphō, “write”). By surface analysis, orto- + -grafia.

parole.significato: oregano (Origanum vulgare, a herb of the mint family)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin orīganum, from Ancient Greek ὀρίγανον (oríganon). Doublet of orégão
From Latin ostrea, from Ancient Greek ὄστρεον (óstreon).
From Latin aura, from Ancient Greek αὔρα (aúra). Doublet of aura, which was borrowed.

From Old Galician-Portuguese palavra, with hyperthesis from earlier paravra, paravla, from Late Latin parabola (“speech”), from Latin parabola (“comparison, illustration”), from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ, “comparison; parable”). Doublet of parábola, a borrowing.

parole.significato: lecture, talk (spoken lesson or exposition, usually delivered to a group)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin palaestra, from Ancient Greek παλαίστρα (palaístra, “wrestling school”).
Learned borrowing from Latin Palladium (the image of Pallas that protected Troy), from Ancient Greek Παλλάδιον (Palládion), from Παλλάς (Pallás).

parole.significato: panacea (remedy believed to cure all disease)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin panacēa, Ancient Greek πανάκεια (panákeia), from πανακής (panakḗs, “all-healing”), from πᾶν (pân, “all”) + ἄκος (ákos, “cure”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Possibly; modificatore <unc> nel legame; nodo incerto nell'albero
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese panela, from Vulgar Latin *pannella, from Late Latin panna, possibly from Latin patina (“frying pan”). Related to English pan. Cognate with Sicilian panneḍḍa.

parole.significato: pantheon (all the gods of a particular religion)
parole.testo: From Latin Pantheon, from Ancient Greek Πάνθειον (Pántheion, “a temple of all gods”), neuter of πάνθειος (pántheios, “of or common to all gods”), from παν- (pan-, “all, everything”) + θεῖος (theîos, “of or for the gods”), from θεός (theós, “god”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese papa, probably borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin papas, from Ancient Greek πάπας (pápas, “bishop, patriarch”), variant of πάππας (páppas, “father”).

parole.significato: papyrus (Cyperus papyrus, a plant native to the Nile valley)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin papȳrus, borrowed from Ancient Greek πάπυρος (pápuros). Doublet of papel and pavio.
From Late Latin paradīgma (“paradigm”), from Ancient Greek παράδειγμα (parádeigma, “pattern”).
From Latin paradīsiacus, from Ancient Greek παραδεισιακός (paradeisiakós), from παράδεισος (parádeisos, “paradise”) + -ακός (-akós, adjective-forming suffix).

Learned borrowing from New Latin parallēlepipedum, from Ancient Greek παραλληλεπίπεδος (parallēlepípedos, “with parallel surfaces”), from παράλληλος (parállēlos, “parallel”) + ἐπίπεδος (epípedos, “plane”).

parole.significato: parallel (of two or more (straight) lines, (flat) surfaces etc: equally distant from one another at all points)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin parallēlus, from Ancient Greek παράλληλος (parállēlos), from παρά (pará, “beside”) + ἄλληλος (állēlos, “one another”).
Borrowed from Latin paralyticus, from Ancient Greek παραλυτικός (paralutikós, “paralyzed”).
From Latin paranymphus, from Ancient Greek παράνυμφος (paránumphos).
From Latin parasitus, from Ancient Greek παράσιτος (parásitos, “person who eats at the table of another”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese parayso, from Latin paradīsus, from Ancient Greek παράδεισος (parádeisos), from Proto-Iranian *paridayjah.

parole.significato: paroxysm (a random or sudden outburst of activity)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin paroxysmus, from Ancient Greek παροξυσμός (paroxusmós).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ). Doublet of palavra. The mathematical sense is taken from New Latin or directly from Greek.
From Scientific Latin parenchyma, from Ancient Greek παρέγχυμα (parénkhuma).
From Late Latin parenthesis (“addition of a letter to a syllable in a word”), from Ancient Greek παρένθεσις (parénthesis).
From Late Latin parochia, from Ancient Greek παροικία (paroikía, “a dwelling abroad”), from παρά (pará, “beside”) + οἶκος (oîkos, “house”).
From Late Latin pasmus, from Ancient Greek σπασμός (spasmós, “spasm”). Doublet of espasmo.

parole.significato: dough (mix of flour and other ingredients)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese pasta, from Late Latin pasta (“dough, pastry cake, paste”), from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá). Cognate with Galician pasta.
Learned borrowing from Latin patriōta, from Ancient Greek πατριώτης (patriṓtēs, “of the same country”). By surface analysis, pátria + -ota.

From Latin paedagōgus, from Ancient Greek παιδαγωγός (paidagōgós).
From Old Galician-Portuguese pedaço, from Latin pittacium, from Ancient Greek πιττάκιον (pittákion). Compare Spanish pedazo.

From Old Galician-Portuguese peego, from Latin pelagus (“sea”), from Ancient Greek πέλαγος (pélagos). Doublet of pélago.

parole.significato: pelican (any of various seabirds of the family Pelecanidae)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin pelicānus (“pelican”), from Ancient Greek πελεκάνος (pelekános).
From Latin peltastae, from Ancient Greek πελταστής (peltastḗs).
From Latin pelagicus, from Ancient Greek πελαγικός (pelagikós).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese pena (displacing pẽa), from Latin poena, from Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ, “penalty, fine, bloodmoney”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷoynéh₂.
From Late Latin pentagōnum, from Ancient Greek πεντάγωνον (pentágōnon, “pentagon”), neuter form of πεντάγωνος (pentágōnos, “five-angled”). By surface analysis, penta- + -gono.
From Latin peplus, from Ancient Greek πέπλος (péplos).
From Latin perca (“perch”), from Ancient Greek πέρκη (pérkē, “perch”).

parole.significato: partridge (any bird of the genera Perdix or Alectoris)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese perdiz, from Latin perdīcem (“partridge”), from Ancient Greek πέρδιξ (pérdix, “partridge”). Compare Galician, Asturian, and Spanish perdiz.

parole.significato: parchment (writing material made of animal skin)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese pergaminho, from Late Latin pergamēna, borrowed from Ancient Greek Περγαμηνὴ (διφθέρα) (Pergamēnḕ (diphthéra), “Pergamene hide”), from Πέργαμον (Pérgamon) + -ηνός (-ēnós). Doublet of pergameno. Compare Galician pergameo and Spanish pergamino.

parole.significato: perigee (the point on the Moon's orbit, on the orbit of an artificial satellite or on the Sun's orbit in apparent annua…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin perigaeum, from Ancient Greek περίγειον (perígeion).

parole.significato: Persian (member of ethnic group native to the Iranian plateau)
parole.testo: From Latin Persa, Persēs, from Ancient Greek Πέρσης (Pérsēs), from Old Persian 𐎱𐎠𐎼𐎿 (p-a-r-s /⁠Pārsa⁠/, “Persian”). Displaced Old Galician-Portuguese perssião.
Learned borrowing from New Latin periodus, a learned borrowing from Ancient Greek περῐ́οδος (perĭ́odos, “going round in a circle, periodic recurrence”).

From Latin paeān (“a hymn, especially a victory hymn, to Apollo or another god”), from Ancient Greek παιᾱ́ν (paiā́n, “a chant or song, especially a thanksgiving or victory hymn, to Apollo under the name Παιᾱ́ν (Paiā́n)”), from the phrase Ἰὼ Παιᾱ́ν (Iṑ Paiā́n, “O Paean!, Thanks to Paean!”).
From Latin pygargus from Ancient Greek πύγαργος (púgargos), a compound of Ancient Greek πῡγή (pūgḗ, “rump”) + ἀργός (argós, “white”).

parole.significato: pygmy (a member of various African peoples noted for their low stature)
parole.testo: From Latin pygmaeus, from Ancient Greek πυγμαῖος (pugmaîos).
Learned borrowing from Latin pylōrus, from Ancient Greek πυλωρός (pulōrós, “gatekeeper”).
From Latin pinacothēca, from Ancient Greek πινακοθήκη (pinakothḗkē, “picture gallery”, literally “tablet box”).

parole.significato: pirate (person who commits robbery at sea against other ships)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pīrāta, from Ancient Greek πειρατής (peiratḗs), from πεῖρα (peîra, “trial, attempt, plot”).
From Latin Pyrenaeus, from Ancient Greek Πῡρηναῖος (Pūrēnaîos).

From Latin pȳramis, from Ancient Greek πῡραμίς (pūramís).
Learned borrowing from New Latin placenta, from Latin placenta (“cake”), from Ancient Greek πλακόεντα (plakóenta), accusative of πλακόεις (plakóeis, “flat”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese planeta f or m, from Latin planēta, from Ancient Greek πλανήτης (planḗtēs) variant of πλάνης (plánēs, “wanderer, planet”), from πλανάω (planáō, “wander about, stray”), of unknown origin.

parole.significato: stalls (seat in a theatre close to and about level with the stage)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin platēa, from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa, “flat, level”). Compare the inherited doublet praça (“plaza”), also present in Italian platea, piazza, and Spanish platea, plaza.
Borrowed from Late Latin pleonasmus, from Ancient Greek πλεονασμός (pleonasmós), from πλεονάζω (pleonázō, “to be superfluous”), from πλείων (pleíōn, “more”).

parole.significato: plinth (block or slab upon which a column or other structure stands)
parole.testo: From Late Latin plinthus, from Ancient Greek πλίνθος (plínthos, “brick”).
From Latin plasticus (“of molding”), from Ancient Greek πλαστικός (plastikós), from πλάσσειν (plássein, “to mold, form”).

parole.significato: plane (any tree of the genus Platanus)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin platanus, from Ancient Greek πλάτανος (plátanos).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin pneumonia, from Ancient Greek πνευμονία (pneumonía).
From Latin poēma, from Ancient Greek ποίημα (poíēma), from ποιέω (poiéō, “to make”).
From Latin poesis, from Ancient Greek ποίησις (poíēsis, “production, composition”).
Borrowed from Latin poēta, from Ancient Greek ποιητής (poiētḗs).

parole.significato: polygamy (the practice of having multiple spouses or partners)
parole.testo: From Late Latin polygamia, from Ancient Greek πολυγαμία (polugamía), itself from πολύγαμος (polúgamos, “married to many”), from πολύς (polús, “many”) + γάμος (gámos, “marriage”). By surface analysis, poli- + -gamia.
Learned borrowing from Latin polus (“pole”), from Ancient Greek πόλος (pólos, “axis of rotation”).

Learned borrowing from Late Latin polītīa, borrowed from Ancient Greek πολῑτείᾱ (polīteíā), from πολῑ́της (polī́tēs, “citizen”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, abstract noun–forming suffix).
Borrowed from Latin polīticus, from Ancient Greek πολιτικός (politikós).

parole.significato: pore (a tiny opening in the skin)
parole.testo: From Latin porus, from Ancient Greek πόρος (póros, “passage”).

From Latin pragmatĭcus, from Ancient Greek πραγματικός (pragmatikós).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese prata. Compare Galician prata and Spanish plata. See also the related prato and chato.

parole.significato: to practice (repeat an activity as a way of improving one’s skill)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin prāctica (“practical affairs; business”), from Ancient Greek πρᾱκτική (prāktikḗ, “practice, experience”), from πρακτικός (praktikós, “practical”), from πράσσω (prássō, “to do”).

parole.significato: plaza (a public square or open area in front of a building or a place)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese praça, plaça, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin platēa, from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa), shortening of πλατεῖα ὁδός (plateîa hodós, “broad way”). parole.significato: prism (polyhedron with parallel ends of the same size and shape)
parole.testo: Latin prisma, from Ancient Greek πρίσμα (prísma).

parole.significato: problem (difficulty that has to be resolved or dealt with)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin problēma, from Ancient Greek πρόβλημα (próblēma, “obstacle”).
Borrowed from Late Latin problēmaticus, from Ancient Greek προβληματικός (problēmatikós), from πρόβλημα (próblēma, “outjutting, barrier, problem”).
Learned borrowing from Latin prophētīa.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese profeta, a learned borrowing from Latin prophēta, borrowed from Ancient Greek προφήτης (prophḗtēs), from προ- (pro-, “before”) + φημί (phēmí, “to say”) + -της (-tēs, “-er”, masculine agent-noun suffix).

parole.significato: prognosis (forecast of the future course of a disease)
parole.testo: From Latin prognōsis, borrowed from Ancient Greek πρόγνωσῐς (prógnōsĭs).

parole.significato: prognostic (being a forecast of future development)
parole.testo: From Latin prognosticus, from Ancient Greek προγνωστικός (prognōstikós, “foreknowing”), from προ- (pro-) + γνωστικός (gnōstikós, “of or for knowing, good at knowing”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin programma, from Ancient Greek πρόγραμμα (prógramma).

From programa (“programme”) + -ção (“-tion”), from Late Latin programma (“a proclamation, edict”), from Ancient Greek πρόγραμμα (prógramma, “a written public notice, an edict”), from προγράφω (prográphō, “to set forth as a public notice”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + γράφω (gráphō, “to write”).

parole.significato: prosopography (a study of the individuals in a group of people within a specific context and their relationships)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prosōpographia.

parole.significato: proselyte (one who has recently converted to a religion or doctrine)
parole.testo: From Late Latin prosēlytus, from Ancient Greek προσήλυτος (prosḗlutos).

parole.significato: prosody (study of rhythm and other attributes in speech)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin prosōdia.

From Latin practicus, from Ancient Greek πρακτικός (praktikós, “of or relating to action, concerned with action or business, active, practical”), from πράσσω (prássō, “to do”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese prologo, borrowed from Latin prologus, from Ancient Greek πρόλογος (prólogos).

From Medieval Latin prostata, from Ancient Greek προστάτης (prostátēs, “one standing before, protector”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to stand”).

parole.significato: prosthesis (artificial replacement for a body part)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin prothesis, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: circumnavigation, periplus (navigation around a sea or the maritime coasts of a country)
parole.testo: From Latin periplūs, from Ancient Greek περῐ́πλους (perĭ́plous).

parole.significato: polyp (abnormal growth protruding from a mucous membrane)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin polypus. Doublet of polvo.
From Latin pūnicus (“Punic”), from poenicus (“Phoenician”), from Ancient Greek Φοῖνιξ (Phoînix, “Phoenician”).

parole.significato: a colour between purple and red
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin purpura, from Ancient Greek πορφύρα (porphúra).

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese querubin (“cherub”), from Latin cherūbīm, from Ancient Greek χερουβίν (kheroubín), from Biblical Hebrew כרֻבִים (keruvím), plural indefinite form of כְּרוּב (kerúv), from a Proto-Semitic source.
From Latin chylus, from Ancient Greek χυλός (khulós, “animal or plant juice”).

parole.significato: chyme (partly digested food passed from the stomach to the duodenum)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin chymus, from Ancient Greek χυμός (khumós, “juice”).
Learned borrowing from New Latin chiro-.
Borrowed from Latin chiton, from Ancient Greek χιτών (khitṓn).

parole.significato: radish (Raphanus raphanistrum subsp. sativus, syn. Raphanus sativus, a plant)

parole.significato: clockmaker; watchmaker (person who makes and repairs clocks and watches)
parole.testo: From relojo (“clock”) + -eiro (“-eer”), from Latin hōrologium (“sundial”), from Ancient Greek ὡρολόγιον (hōrológion).

parole.significato: rheme (part of a sentence that provides new information)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin rhema, from Ancient Greek ῥῆμα (rhêma).

parole.significato: to repose; to rest, to relax
parole.testo: From Late Latin repausāre, from Latin re- (“again”) + pausō (“to pause, to rest”), from pausa (“pause”), from Ancient Greek παῦσις (paûsis).

parole.significato: rhetoric (art of using language for persuasion)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin rhētorica.

parole.significato: rhetorical (relating to or reminiscent of rhetoric)
parole.testo: From Latin rhētoricus, from Ancient Greek ῥητορικός (rhētorikós).

parole.significato: rheumatic (relating to, suffering from or characterised by rheumatism)
parole.testo: From Late Latin rheumaticus, from Ancient Greek ῥευματικός (rheumatikós).
From Latin rhīnocerōntem, from Ancient Greek ῥινόκερως (rhinókerōs), from ῥίς (rhís, “nose”) + κέρας (kéras, “horn”).
From Latin rhythmus, from Ancient Greek ῥυθμός (rhuthmós), from ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”).

parole.significato: to snore (to breathe during sleep with harsh noises)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese roncar, from Latin rhonchāre, from rhonchus, from Ancient Greek ῥόγχος (rhónkhos, “snoring”), of imitative origin.
From Latin rhoncus, from Ancient Greek ῥόγχος (rhónkhos).

parole.significato: hurdy-gurdy (medieval instrument with a wheel that vibrates its strings)

parole.significato: sardine (any of several small, edible species of herring)

parole.significato: Semite (member of the Semites, an ethnic group of the Middle East)
parole.testo: From Sem + -ita, from Late Latin Sēm, from Ancient Greek Σήμ (Sḗm), from Biblical Hebrew שם (šēm). Compare German Semit, New Latin Sēmīta, French sémite.

parole.significato: mermaid (mythological woman with a fish's tail)

From Latin syllepsis, from Ancient Greek σύλληψις (súllēpsis).

parole.significato: syllogism (inference from two or more premises)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin syllogismus, from Ancient Greek συλλογισμός (sullogismós, “inference, conclusion”).
From Latin syllabĭcus, from Ancient Greek συλλαβικός (sullabikós).

parole.significato: symmetry (correspondence on either side of a dividing line, plane, center or axis)

From Late Latin sympathīa, from Ancient Greek συμπάθεια (sumpátheia).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese sinagoga, from Latin synagōga, from Ancient Greek συναγωγή (sunagōgḗ, “assembly, gathering”), from συνάγω (sunágō, “to bring together”).

parole.significato: syncellus (an office of the Eastern Orthodox Church)
parole.testo: From Latin syncellus (“sharing the same cell”), from Ancient Greek σύγκελλος (súnkellos), albeit κέλλα (kélla) derives from Latin cella.

Borrowed from Latin symphōnia, from Ancient Greek σῠμφωνῐ́ᾱ (sŭmphōnĭ́ā). Doublet of sanfona.

Learned borrowing from Latin synōnymum, from Ancient Greek συνώνυμον (sunṓnumon), neuter singular form of συνώνυμος (sunṓnumos, “synonymous”).

parole.significato: syrinx (very old flute, with transverse wind, consisting of a series of tubes that produce a scale, Pan flute)

parole.significato: systematic (belonging to or relating to a system)

parole.significato: Sapphic (relating to the Greek poetess Sappho or her poetry)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sapphicus, from Ancient Greek Σαπφικός (Sapphikós), from Σαπφώ (Sapphṓ). By surface analysis, Safo + -ico.
From Latin satyrus, from Ancient Greek σάτυρος (sáturos).

parole.significato: cuttlefish (any squid-like mollusc of the genus Sepia)
