parole.testo: From Latin tagenia, from Ancient Greek [Term?].

parole.significato: talent (Classical unit of weight and money)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin talentum (“a Grecian weight; a talent of money”), from Ancient Greek τάλαντον (tálanton, “balance; a particular weight, especially of gold; sum of money; a talent”), from Proto-Indo-European *tl̥h₂ent-, from *telh₂-.
From Latin thallus, from Ancient Greek θαλλός (thallós).
From Latin tarsus (“tarsus”), from Ancient Greek ταρσός (tarsós, “flat surface used for drying”).
From Medieval Latin thaumaturgus, from Ancient Greek θαυματουργός (thaumatourgós).

parole.significato: theater (a place or building, consisting of a stage and seating, in which an audience gathers to watch plays, musical p…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin theātrum (“theatre; stage”), from Ancient Greek θέατρον (théatron, “a place for viewing”), from θεάομαι (theáomai, “to see; to watch; to observe”). Compare Sicilian tiatru.

parole.significato: theca (covering or membrane, usually of a fibrous nature, that surrounds certain organs)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin thēca, from Ancient Greek θήκη (thḗkē).
From Latin thema, from Ancient Greek θέμα (théma). Doublet of tema.

parole.significato: theme; topic; subject (what something is about)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin thema, from Ancient Greek θέμα (théma). Doublet of teima.

parole.significato: tendon (tissue that connects a muscle with a bone)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin tendō, tendōnem, from Ancient Greek τένων (ténōn, “sinew, tendon”)
From Latin theologia, from Ancient Greek θεολογία (theología). By surface analysis, teo- + -logia.
From Latin theologicus, from Ancient Greek θεολογικός (theologikós).

parole.significato: theory (coherent set of statements attempting to explain observed phenomena)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin theōria (“theory”), from Ancient Greek θεωρία (theōría, “contemplation; speculation; a looking at; things looked at”), from θεωρέω (theōréō, “to look at, to view, to consider, to examine”), from θεωρός (theōrós, “spectator”).
From New Latin therapīa, from Ancient Greek θεραπεία (therapeía).
From Latin terebinthus, from Ancient Greek τερέβινθος (terébinthos).
Learned borrowing from Latin thēsaurus (“treasure; hoard”), from Ancient Greek θησαυρός (thēsaurós, “storehouse; treasure”). Doublet of tesouro.
Learned borrowing from Latin thesis, from Ancient Greek θέσις (thésis, “a proposition, a statement, a thing laid down, thesis in rhetoric, thesis in prosody”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese tesouro, from Latin thēsaurus (“treasure; hoard”), from Ancient Greek θησαυρός (thēsaurós, “storehouse; treasure”). Doublet of the borrowing tesauro.

parole.significato: theta (name of the Greek letter Θ θ)
parole.testo: From Latin thēta, in turn borrowed from Ancient Greek θῆτα (thêta, “theta”).

parole.significato: tetrarch (governor of subdivision of a province)
parole.testo: From Late Latin tetrarcha, from Latin tetrarchēs, from Ancient Greek τετράρχης (tetrárkhēs). By surface analysis, tetra- + -arca.
From Latin theologus, from Ancient Greek θεολόγος (theológos).

parole.significato: aunt (sister of someone's father or mother, or an uncle's wife)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese tia, from Late Latin thīa, from Ancient Greek θεία (theía).
Borrowed from Latin tiāra, from Ancient Greek τιάρα (tiára).

parole.significato: cattail (any of several perennial herbs of the genus Typha)
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin typha, from Ancient Greek τύφη (túphē, “Typha angustata, a species of cattail”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese tygris, a learned borrowing from Latin tigris, borrowed from Ancient Greek τίγρις (tígris).

parole.significato: thymus (ductless gland located behind the breastbone)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin thymus.

parole.significato: uncle (brother of someone's father or mother, or an aunt's husband)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese tio, from Late Latin thīus, from Ancient Greek θεῖος (theîos). Compare Galician and Spanish tío, Italian zio, Sardinian tiu.

parole.significato: kind; sort; type (grouping based on shared characteristics)
parole.testo: From Latin typus (“figure; type”), from Ancient Greek τύπος (túpos, “mark”), from τύπτω (túptō, “to poke”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewp-.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese tirano, borrowed from Latin tyrannus, borrowed from Ancient Greek τύραννος (túrannos, “absolute ruler”).
From Latin thyrsus, from Ancient Greek θύρσος (thúrsos). Doublet of torso and possibly troço.

parole.significato: tyrannical (of, or relating to tyranny, of a tyrant)
parole.testo: From Latin tyrannicus, from Ancient Greek τυραννικός (turannikós).

parole.significato: titan (any of the giant primordial gods that were replaced by the Olympian gods)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Tītān, from Ancient Greek Τιτάν (Titán).

parole.significato: tone; pitch (property of sound determined by the frequency)
parole.testo: Probably a semi-learned borrowing from Latin tonus (and influenced by som; compare the Spanish ton, variant of the standard tono, which underwent a similar change, influenced by son, respectively), from Ancient Greek τόνος (tónos, “tone”), from τείνω (teínō, “to stretch”). Cf. also trom, a possible

parole.significato: volume, tome (book which is part of a series)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tomus (“section of larger work”), from Ancient Greek τόμος (tómos, “section, roll of papyrus, volume”), from τέμνω (témnō, “to cut, to separate”).
From Latin topazius, from Ancient Greek τόπαζος (tópazos).
Inherited from Latin tornum (“lathe”), from Ancient Greek τόρνος (tórnos, “lathe”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese torre (“tower”), from Latin turrem (“tower”), from Ancient Greek τύρσις (túrsis, “tower, bastion”). Cognate with Galician, Spanish, Catalan, Occitan, Italian, and Ladino torre and French tour.
From Medieval Latin thōrācicus, from Ancient Greek θωρακικός (thōrakikós, “suffering in the chest, of the thorax”), from θώραξ (thṓrax, “thorax”).

parole.significato: tragedy (work in which the main character is suffers negative consequences)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin tragoedia, from Ancient Greek τραγῳδῐ́ᾱ (tragōidĭ́ā).
Learned borrowing from Latin trifolium, a calque of Ancient Greek τρίφυλλον (tríphullon). Doublet of the inherited trevo.

parole.significato: trigonometry (branch of mathematics dealing with triangles)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin trigōnometria, from Ancient Greek τρίγωνον (trígōnon, “triangle”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”).
From Vulgar Latin *triblus, from Latin tribulus, from Ancient Greek τρίβολος (tríbolos).
From Latin Trītōne, from Ancient Greek Τρῑ́των (Trī́tōn).
Learned borrowing from Latin Trōglodytae (“cave-dwelling people”), from Ancient Greek τρωγλοδύτης (trōglodútēs, “one who dwells in holes”), from τρώγλη (trṓglē, “hole”) + δύω (dúō, “to get into”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese trono (“throne”), borrowed from Latin thronus (“throne”) and displacing the inherited trõo, from Ancient Greek θρόνος (thrónos, “throne, seat”).
From Late Latin tropologicus, from Ancient Greek τροπολογικός (tropologikós). By surface analysis, tropologia + -ico.

parole.significato: trout (fish in Salmonidae which spawns more than once)
parole.testo: From Late Latin tructa, of uncertain origin, possibly from Ancient Greek τρώκτης (trṓktēs). Compare Galician troita.
From Latin tragicus, from Ancient Greek τραγικός (tragikós).
Learned borrowing from Latin trepanum, from Ancient Greek τρύπανον (trúpanon).
From Latin tribas, from Ancient Greek τριβάς (tribás), from τρίβω (tríbō, “to rub”).

parole.significato: tomb (small building or vault for the remains of the dead)
parole.testo: From Late Latin tumba (possibly borrowed), from Ancient Greek τύμβος (túmbos).
Borrowed from Latin turba.

parole.significato: censer; thurible (religious ornamental container for burning incense)
parole.testo: From Latin thūribulum (“censer”), equivalent to thūs, thūris (“incense”) (from Ancient Greek θύος (thúos, “burnt offering”)) + -bulum (instrumental suffix).
Learned borrowing from Latin thalamus, from Ancient Greek θάλαμος (thálamos).
Learned borrowing from Latin taenia.

parole.significato: eardrum; tympanum (membrane that separates the outer ear from the middle ear)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tympanum (“drum”), from Ancient Greek τύμπανον (túmpanon, “drum”). Doublet of timbre.
From Latin thōrax, from Ancient Greek θώραξ (thṓrax, “a breastplate, cuirass, corslet”).

parole.significato: poison (substance harmful to a living organism)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin toxicum (“arrow poison”), from Ancient Greek τοξικόν (toxikón, “arrow poison”), from τοξικός (toxikós, “pertaining to bows”), from τόξον (tóxon, “bow”).
From Latin ūranographia, from Ancient Greek οὐρανογραφία (ouranographía). By surface analysis, urano- + -grafia.
From Latin ūrēthra, from Ancient Greek οὐρήθρα (ourḗthra, “urethra”), from οὐρέω (ouréō, “to urinate”).

From New Latin Utopia, the name of a fictional island, possessing a seemingly perfect socio-politico-legal system in the book Utopia (1516) by Sir Thomas More. Coined from Ancient Greek οὐ (ou, “not, no”) + τόπος (tópos, “place, region”).
Learned borrowing from New Latin Xenarthra, from Ancient Greek ξένος (xénos, “foreign, alien”) + ἄρθρον (árthron, “joint”).

parole.significato: special care and dedication for someone or something
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin zēlus (“zeal”), from Ancient Greek ζῆλος (zêlos, “eager rivalry”). Doublet of cio, which was inherited.
From Latin zeugma, from Ancient Greek ζεῦγμα (zeûgma, “bond, yoking”).

parole.significato: zodiac (region of the celestial sphere corresponding to the apparent path of the sun)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin zōdiacus, from Ancient Greek ζῳδιακός (zōidiakós).

parole.significato: zone (in a broad geographic or geometric sense)
parole.testo: From Latin zōna (“girdle, zone”), from Ancient Greek ζώνη (zṓnē, “belt, sash, zone”).

parole.significato: zotheca (cabinet, in ancient Roman dwellings, for study, rest or nap)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin zotheca, from Ancient Greek ζωθήκη (zōthḗkē).
Borrowed from Latin zephyrus, from Ancient Greek Ζέφυρος (Zéphuros).

parole.significato: abacus (instrument for performing arithmetical calculations by sliding balls on wires, or counters in grooves)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin abacus (“board”), from Ancient Greek ἄβαξ (ábax, “board”), from Hebrew אבק (abák, “dust”).
Borrowed from New Latin acarus, from Ancient Greek ἄκαρι (ákari, “cheese mite, tick”), from ἀκαρής (akarḗs, “tiny”).
Ultimately from Latin achātēs, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓χᾱ́της (ăkhā́tēs).
Borrowed from Latin Arabs, from Ancient Greek Ἄραψ (Áraps, “Arab, Arabian”), from Arabic عَرَب (ʕarab). Doublet of alarve.

parole.significato: Arctic (of or relating to the Arctic)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin arcticus, from Ancient Greek ἀρκτικός (arktikós, “northern, of the (Great) Bear”), from ἄρκτος (árktos, “bear, Ursa Major”).
Borrowed from Latin aspidem, from Ancient Greek ἀσπίς (aspís).
Learned borrowing from Latin atomus (“smallest particle”), from Ancient Greek ἄτομος (átomos, “indivisible”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + τέμνω (témnō, “to cut”).

parole.significato: anchor (object that moors a vessel to the sea bottom)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese ancora, from Latin ancora, from Ancient Greek ἄγκυρα (ánkura), from Proto-Indo-European *ang- (“corner, hirn”).
Learned borrowing from Latin amphora, from Ancient Greek ἀμφορεύς (amphoreús).

parole.significato: epic (of, or relating to, an epic)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin epicus.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin epocha, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐποχή (epokhḗ).
Learned borrowing from Latin aethēr (“the upper pure, bright air”), from Ancient Greek αἰθήρ (aithḗr, “upper air”), from αἴθω (aíthō, “to burn, shine”).

parole.significato: ethics (study of principles governing right and wrong conduct)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin ethica, from Ancient Greek ἠθική (ēthikḗ), feminine of ἠθικός (ēthikós, “of or for morals, moral, expressing character”), from ἦθος (êthos, “character, moral nature”).
Borrowed from Latin ēthicus, from Ancient Greek ἠθικός (ēthikós).
Borrowed from Latin etymon, from Ancient Greek ἔτυμον (étumon, “the true sense of a word according to its origin”), from ἔτυμος (étumos, “true, real, actual”).

parole.significato: ethnic (related to a group of people having common origins)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ethnicus (“pagan; heathen”), from Ancient Greek ἐθνικός (ethnikós, “of or for a nation, heathen”), from ἔθνος (éthnos, “a company”, later “a people or nation, heathens”).
Borrowed from Latin emphasis, from Ancient Greek ἔμφασις (émphasis, “significance”).
Learned borrowing from Latin ecstasis, from Ancient Greek ἔκστᾰσῐς (ékstăsĭs).
Learned borrowing from Latin īconem (“icon”), from Ancient Greek εἰκών (eikṓn, “likeness, image, portrait”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese idolo, borrowed from Latin īdōlum, from Ancient Greek εἴδωλον (eídōlon, “image, idol”), from εἶδος (eîdos, “form”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to see”).
Learned borrowing from Latin īleus, from Ancient Greek εἰλεός (eileós).

parole.significato: The name of the Latin script letter Y/y.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ypsilon (“upsilon”), from Ancient Greek ὖ ψιλόν (û psilón, “upsilon”) (modern Greek ύψιλον (ýpsilon)), from ὖ (û) + ψιλός (psilós).

parole.significato: iris (plant of the genus Iris), or its flower
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin iris, Ancient Greek ἶρις (îris, “rainbow”).
Learned borrowing from Latin obelus, from Ancient Greek ὀβελός (obelós).
Learned borrowing from Latin obolus, from Ancient Greek ὀβολός (obolós), from ὀβελός (obelós, “spit, rod”).

parole.significato: oil (liquid substance extracted from animals, vegetals, or minerals)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin oleum (“oil, olive oil”), from Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion, “olive oil”), from ἐλαία (elaía, “olive”), from Proto-Indo-European *loiu̯om.
Borrowed from Latin onyx, from Ancient Greek ὄνυξ (ónux, “claw; onyx”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃nogʰ-.
Inherited from Late Latin orphănus, from Ancient Greek ὀρφανός (orphanós, “without parents, fatherless”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃órbʰos.
Inherited from Latin organum, from Ancient Greek ὄργανον (órganon, “organ, instrument, tool”), from Proto-Indo-European *werǵ- (“work”).

parole.significato: oryx (any of several African antelopes of the genus Oryx)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin oryx, from Ancient Greek ὄρυξ (órux, “a pickax; an oryx (the antelope)”).
